It was recorded as "prototype.html routes ?pane=evals and titles the board Evals; the running app's window title reads back Checks". The second half is false. `prototype.html:600` declares the sidebar entry as `{id:'evals',t:'Checks',ic:'evals'}` — the route **id** is `evals` and the **title** is `Checks` — and the board's own header draws the selected suite (`pr-summariser · 8 cases`) rather than a board name at all. An id and a title are different fields that the design is entitled to disagree on, so a tie pass that compares one to the other reports a rename wherever a route is not named after its board. (1) Activity's and Cleanup's header action. `prototype.html:716` and `:930` both call it `Reset history…`; the build shipped `Reset call history…`, which is a DIFFERENT SLOT's wording — the Danger section of Settings at `:999`, which this app does not draw. `CleanupPresentation.resetLabel` is now `Reset history…` and both headers call it. (2) Skills' header action. `prototype.html:786` calls it `Add marketplace…`; the board shipped `Manage marketplaces…` while `MenuCommand.addMarketplace` had always said `Add marketplace…`, so the menu item and the button that open the SAME SHEET named it two different things. Stated once as `SkillPresentation.marketplacesAction` and read by all three call sites, so they cannot drift again — and the test asserts the literal is absent from both files rather than that the strings happen to match today. Armed: reverting the label reads `the header action is called Reset call history…`, and restoring either literal trips the drift assertion.

defect.title: the ios-glass lane's tab-navigation assertion does not reproduce
defect.detail:
Three consecutive runs, same build, same booted iPhone 16 Pro, no product change between them: run 1 failed 3 of 5, runs 2 and 3 failed 4 of 5. The case that moved is `tapping 'X' did not produce a navigation bar titled 'X'` — green for all five tabs in run 1, red on the first tab in runs 2 and 3. The only edit between run 1 and run 2 was adding XCTAttachment captures to a different test, so the code under assertion did not change. A plausible mechanism is DEF-008: the tab button's accessibility identifier is the SF Symbol name while its label is the tab title, so `buttons["Discover"]` resolves on one attribute or the other depending on which the tree publishes first. Not diagnosed further here — this campaign records the instrument's reliability rather than repairing another branch's test. Consequence: the lane's outcome-rung claims are recorded inconclusive, because green twice is the campaign's own bar and this lane did not clear it.

CLOSED 20 Aug 2026. Diagnosed from run 3's exported App UI hierarchy: at the failure the navigation bar's identifier was 'Settings' and the Settings tab carried Selected, so the opening tap had never landed. Run 1 passed because a freshly installed app launches on Discover, making its first selectTab a no-op; runs 2 and 3 restored to Settings and tapped a tab bar that existed but was not yet hittable. Existence is not hittability. `selectTab` now waits on a `hittable == true` predicate and retries the tap up to three times against the tab button's own `isSelected`, which is the tab bar's answer to 'which tab am I on'. Green twice since, across all three affected tests. DEF-008 was not the mechanism.

defect.title: the fixture client's usageSummary ignored the scenario, so Cleanup had no empty state
defect.detail: Found by auditing the other reads once DEF-009 was fixed, not by a failing test — so no case watched it fail and it earns no arming credit. `usageSummary()` returned the recorded four-server summary for every scenario, and it is the only call CleanupBoardModel makes. Under `.empty` the Cleanup board therefore offered four never-used servers to cull on a router with nothing declared. Fixed the same way as DEF-009: `.empty` returns no servers and keeps `since` from the recording, because a router that has been counting since a moment and has nothing to report is a different statement from one with no window at all. Audit result for the record: of the seventeen methods, seven do not branch on the scenario and six of those are writes, where a read-scenario legitimately does not apply and guardFailure() already covers offline/unauthorized/error. The seventh is `server(named:)`, which answers about a server the caller has already named and has no meaningful empty form; no surface calls it.

defect.title: three Mac boards lay out wider than their window, so both edges clip in silence
defect.detail:
**The recorded cause was wrong, and this replaces it.** It said the shutter fired during a board transition and named the fix as a settle in `capture-mac-glass.sh`. Measured 20 Aug 2026 from the accessibility dumps the same script already writes, one per board, beside the pictures:

| board | window | AXSplitGroup | clipped |
|---|---|---|---|
| Servers, Activity, Cleanup, Inbox, Settings | 980pt | 980pt | — |
| Checks | 980pt | 988pt | 8pt |
| Skills | 980pt | 1044pt | 64pt |
| Discover | 980pt | 1119pt | 139pt |

Every window in the run is the same 980x620 and every capture is the same 2096x1376, so no capture rect is wrong and no shutter is early. What differs is the shell **inside** the window: on three boards `NavigationSplitView` lays out wider than the window and centres the excess — the split group's origin moves left by exactly half the overflow in all three cases (180→148 for 64pt, 180→110.5 for 139pt, 180→176 for 8pt), which is what makes the clipping symmetrical. That is why the sidebar's section headers read `unning` and `brary` while the nav rows beside them are whole: the headers sit at a smaller leading inset and fall off first, and the header's trailing controls — `Manage marketplaces.`, `Review 2.3.0…` — fall off the right by the same amount.

So this is a product defect on three boards rather than a lane defect on two captures, and it is worse than recorded: Checks overflows too, by 8pt, which is small enough that nobody reading the picture saw it. The app declares no minimum window width anywhere, so nothing stops a user reaching this state — the campaign's 980pt window is an ordinary size, not a stress case.

The consequence that made it a defect stands unchanged and is now better founded: a clipped capture is admissible for what it shows and silent about what it cut, so a reader cannot tell an absent control from a cropped one. Both witness verdicts that depend on these captures say in their method field that the right-hand controls were read from the accessibility dump instead.

`capture-mac-glass.sh` now prints `board width: examined=14 overflowing=3` every run, with a line naming each board and its excess. Reported rather than enforced, because three boards overflow today and a known red in `make all` either blocks unrelated work or gets its assertion softened.

NOT FIXED, and the fix is a decision rather than a repair. Either the shell declares a minimum window width at least as wide as its widest board — one line, guarantees nothing ever clips, and costs users on small screens a window they cannot shrink — or the three boards compress, which keeps small screens usable and is per-board column work across all three. Discover at 1119pt is the one that decides how much that costs.

PARTLY CLOSED 20 Aug 2026, on `ai/x4`, and the part that is not closed is named rather than left to look finished.

The mechanism turned out to be a chain rather than a board: each row's fixed columns report a hard minimum width, the detail pane sums them, `NavigationSplitView` reports that as its own minimum, and nothing ever reads it back — this app opts into no minimum window size and `windowResizability` defaults to `.automatic` — so the window proposes 980pt and SwiftUI **places** the oversized child with default centre alignment. The symmetry was the tell. Referred to the xAI lane (grok-4.6, xhigh) with the measured table; it named the propagation as the bug, called both listed fixes second-best, and its Q3 answer — placement plus `.automatic` resizability rather than any documented split-view overflow mode — is what the one-line fix then confirmed.

FIXED: `ContentZone` carries `.frame(minWidth: 0, maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)`. Measured on the rebuilt app through the same accessibility channel: all eight boards read `split=980` inside a `window=980`, overflowing 0 of 8, where the same probe on the previous build read 3 of 8. The sidebar is whole again — `Running`, `Library` and the footer readout all render in full where they were `unning` and `brary`. The leading alignment is the deliberate half: it decides who loses when the content still does not fit, and the answer is never the navigation.

STILL OPEN: the boards' content is still wider than the detail pane on those three, so the trailing chrome is cut at the pane's right edge — Discover's search field reads `Search the regis` and a body sentence loses its last word. That is one-edge clipping where it was two, and it is the conventional behaviour of a too-narrow window rather than a split view eating its own sidebar, but it is still content going missing without saying so. Closing it needs the three boards' columns to flex, which is a design decision about what Discover looks like compressed and is the owner's rather than mine.

GUARDED two ways, and the two see different things. `capture-mac-glass.sh` now **fails** on any board whose split group exceeds its window, and refuses to pass on `examined=0`; all three arms were exercised on 20 Aug 2026 — red at 3 of 14, green at 0 of 14, and exit 1 with no dumps at all. `ShellDetailWidthTests` asserts the modifier in `ShellWindow`'s detail column so a revert is red in `make test` rather than on the next glass run. That test's own first version was a detector defect found by arming: it searched the raw source slice, and the modifier it looks for is named in the doc comment three lines above it, so deleting the modifier left the assertion green. Comments are stripped before matching now, and both halves were re-armed separately.

CLOSED 20 Aug 2026, and the second half corrected the first half's diagnosis of *which* content was too wide.

The brief written from the split-group numbers said three boards' table columns needed to flex. A pane-level probe — every leaf's right edge against the window's, read from the same dumps — says otherwise, and it says so only after the probe itself was fixed: the first version read the frame's **y** where it meant **x** and reported clipping on seven of eight boards, which the pixels flatly denied. The Settings capture is whole, and looking at it is what caught the field offset. A frame's last five fields are x, y, w, h and a flag; the split-group gate only ever compared widths, which is why it was right while the leaf probe was wrong.

Corrected, the drivers are:

- **Discover**: content wants 823pt against a 684pt pane. Not the table — cutting `nameColumn` from 216pt to 96pt moved the number by **zero**. It is the controls row: a `.fixedSize()` segmented picker measuring 567pt beside a search field pinned at 240pt.
- **Skills**: 748pt against 684pt, same shape — a 516pt fixed picker and a 216pt pinned field.
- **Checks**: not a content defect at all. Its real content ends at 1152pt inside a 1160pt pane; the only thing past the edge is `KeyClaimProbe`, the `#if DEBUG` test surface A21 names, overhanging by 4pt. It is absent from any build a user runs, and it is what the whole 8pt split-group excess on this board was.

FIXED by giving each board a `searchMinWidth` of four units and declaring the field `minWidth:idealWidth:maxWidth:` rather than `width:`. The picker cannot give a point back — that is what `.fixedSize()` means, and it is right, because a segmented control has nowhere to put a truncated label — so the field is the only control in the row that can. It renders at its full width wherever there is room and shows about eight characters at the narrowest window this app is used at, which is less than anyone wants and more than nothing: it still takes focus, accepts a query and submits.

Measured after: every board reads `split=980` in a `window=980`, and the only leaf past the pane edge on any of the eight is a 1pt scrollbar — plus the Debug key probe's 4pt on Checks. Before, Discover's rows and footnote sat at 1283pt against an edge of 1160.

GUARDED by a second test in `ShellDetailWidthTests`, armed 20 Aug 2026: restoring `.frame(width: DiscoverBoardMetrics.searchWidth)` reddens all three of its assertions. It names the two boards rather than looping over every file, because those are the two the measurement covers — a third board growing this problem is a new measurement, not a case this test silently already made.

defect.title: Activity's 'Reset history…' is specified and never drawn
defect.detail: prototype.html:716 puts 'Reset history…' in the Activity header's right slot, outside the rows conditional, so the design specifies it in both the empty and the populated state. The built board draws no control there at all. Not an honesty guardrail: the router can reset its call history, and the Cleanup board carries 'Reset call history', so the capability exists and only this entry point is missing. Found by the witness pass on SURF-003 and independently by the control differential, which reports designControls=1 buildControls=0 for this board. Distinct from DEF-012, which records the rename of the same action on the board that does carry it.
defect.text: Closed 20 Aug 2026, on the owner's decision that `design/mocks/prototype.html` remains the design of record for the Mac console. `prototype.html:716` puts `Reset history…` in the Activity header's right slot, OUTSIDE the rows conditional, so the design specifies it in the empty state as much as the populated one — which is where somebody actually reaches for it. The built board drew no control there at all, and no honesty guardrail explained the absence: the router can reset its call history and the Cleanup board already carries the same act, so the capability existed and only this entry point was missing. Found by the witness pass on SURF-003 and independently by the control differential (designControls=1 buildControls=0 for this board). FIXED by giving `ActivityModel` a `sheet` and a `resetHistory()` against the same `POST /usage/reset` the Cleanup board uses, and `ActivityBoard.header` a trailing `Button(CleanupPresentation.resetLabel)` disabled until `records` exists — offering it before the router has answered would let a click discard a history nobody has seen. The dialog is `ActivityResetHistorySheet`, whose every string is `CleanupPresentation`'s by call and never by copy, because two boards offering one irreversible act must not describe it two ways (DESIGN.md §6). It passes `window: nil`, which is a fact rather than a gap: Cleanup judges over a span and Activity holds a rolling feed, so the sentence reads "recorded so far". GUARDED by `ActivityResetEntryPointTests`, four assertions, all armed 20 Aug 2026. The header assertion was watched to fail for real before the fix landed — an earlier script aborted before writing the header change, and the test reported `the header draws no reset action` against the tree that had it missing. Removing `_ = try await client.resetUsage()` was rejected as an arm because it fails to compile (typed throws), which is a red for the wrong reason; duplicating the call instead reads `confirming the dialog sent 2 resets`.

defect.title: the ios-glass lane built unsigned, and an unsigned build cannot read the keychain
defect.detail: The lane built with CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO, so the app carried no keychain access group and SecItemCopyMatching returned -34018 errSecMissingEntitlement rather than errSecItemNotFound. PairingRecordStore maps the two apart correctly, so the phone's Settings surface rendered "Can't read this phone's pairing" on a device that had simply never been paired. That was recorded as DEF-X2-b, a suspected product defect. It is a lane defect: built with CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY=- the same assertion passes and the test proceeds 54 lines further. The Makefile now carries a SIGNED variable used by test-ios-glass alone, with the measurement in a comment beside it. The general lesson is the one the campaign keeps relearning — a harness flag can manufacture a finding that reads exactly like the product's own.

defect.title: a red glass run exported no captures, and the naming script policed the wrong population
defect.detail: Two faults in the same step, both found by running the lane red. First, `set -e` killed the recipe at the failing xcodebuild, so the export never ran — the run whose pictures are worth most produced none, and diagnosing a failure meant re-running by hand against a bundle path scraped out of the log. The target now holds the status while the export completes and exits with it afterwards. Second, once the export did run, name-glass-attachments.py treated XCTest's own diagnostics as evidence: a red run attaches a Debug description per failed query, two of those were byte-identical because they describe the same query twice, and its shared-image check stopped the run half-renamed. The check is right and its population was wrong. PhoneGlassTests now prefixes every attachment it takes with GLASS-CAPTURE:, so the split is declared by the producer rather than inferred from filename shape, diagnostics are kept under diagnostics/, and nothing is renamed until every check has passed.

defect.title: the phone rebuilt two owned objects inside body, resetting the pairing flow
defect.detail:
Two instances of one mistake, found together. **The camera adapter** was constructed in `MCPRouterIOSApp.body`; `LiveCameraAuthorization` is a fieldless struct so a fresh one per render cost nothing and hid it, and the moment the lane asked for `FixtureCameraAuthorization` — an actor — the identity changed under the flow on every body pass. Stored once as a `let` beside `storage`, which was already stored for the same reason.

**The pairing model** was the real defect. `PhoneSettingsScreen` built `PairingFlowModel(pairing:camera:store:)` inline inside its `navigationDestination` closure, and `PairingFlowView` takes it as `@Bindable` — which observes an object someone else owns rather than owning one. So every re-render of the Settings screen replaced the model, and `step`'s initial value is `.scan`, so each replacement discarded whatever `start()` had decided and put the scanner back. Now held in `@State` on the screen and created in `onPair`, before `isPairing` is set.

This is a product defect and not a harness artefact: on a phone whose camera has not been asked for yet, the pre-prompt that explains what the camera is for can be replaced by the scanner it was meant to precede, and that scanner has no permission to show anything. It was invisible for as long as it existed because the simulator reports camera access as `.authorized`, which makes `start()` set `.scan` — the same value the reset produced. Two wrongs agreeing is why no host test could see it: the fault is in view composition, and only the on-glass lane exercises that. Left open as a standing note: `Step`'s default of `.scan` is a second hazard of the same shape, since a slow `current()` shows the scanner and then swaps. Fixing that needs an undecided case and is a design call rather than a repair.

defect.title: the ios-glass lane shared a simulator, so another project's app received its taps
defect.detail:
The device picker listed every available iPhone and sorted `state != 'Booted'` first — it *preferred* a device somebody else had already booted. On a machine driving simulators for more than one project, XCUITest's taps then arrive at whichever app is frontmost. Measured 20 Aug 2026: five runs failed on a different tab each time, and a screenshot of the 'simulator' showed another project's VPN app mid-onboarding rather than MCP Router. Every one of those failures read as a product defect, and one of them was chased through three hypotheses — hittability, `isSelected` publish timing, machine load — before anyone photographed the device itself. The rule that would have caught it in one step is the campaign's own: prove it ran before reading what it shows, and a screenshot is how you prove it. The lane now creates and owns `MCPRouter-Glass`, and the tab assertion names the app's own XCUIApplication.state in its failure message so a stolen foreground says so.

Two runs were also lost to a device that reported Booted while still doing its post-erase first boot; the target now waits on bootstatus a second time after any boot it issues.

defect.title: the typed pairing path had no way to type
defect.detail:
`TypedEntryView` rendered eight styled boxes, a helper line and a submit button, and no input affordance of any kind — no TextField, no keypad, no focus state. `PairingCodeEntry` had carried `append(contentsOf:)` and `deleteBackward()` since it was written and nothing in the UI called either, so `.disabled(!entry.isComplete)` on the submit button could never become false. The typed path is the documented fallback for every camera state — the source cites A16 — and for `.restricted`, where iOS Settings is a dead end the user may not be able to clear, it is the *primary* recovery. So the one surface a user reaches by deliberately choosing it was the one that could not be completed.

Fixed with a real `TextField` behind the boxes: it carries the system keyboard, hardware keys on iPad, paste and dictation, and it is what `app.textFields` resolves to on glass. Deliberately NOT `.textContentType(.oneTimeCode)` — that AutoFill reads codes out of Messages and Mail, and this code is read off the Mac's own screen, so it would offer suggestions that are always wrong. The boxes became decoration (`accessibilityHidden`) and the field is the single element labelled 'Pairing code', because `children: .ignore` on a display is right and on an editor strips the trait VoiceOver and XCUITest need. Approach checked against an out-of-family lane (grok-4.6, xhigh) before implementing; it named the same shape and the same reason for avoiding `.oneTimeCode`.

Guarded by `PhoneSurfaceTests.testTypedEntryPublishesAFieldToTypeInto`, armed 20 Aug 2026.

defect.title: the typed-entry surface never drew its own headline
defect.detail: `PairingCopy.entry(.typedEntryReady)` has carried `headline: "Enter the code"` since it was written, and `TypedEntryView` drew only `.body`. Every other pairing surface renders its headline. Nothing failed: a headline defined and not drawn leaves no selector, no assertion and no crash — it is the class of defect only a rendered hierarchy can see, which is why the guard is `PhoneSurfaceTests.testEveryPairingPrePromptRendersItsHeadline` over the four pre-prompt states rather than a check on the one view. Armed 20 Aug 2026.

defect.title: the iOS pairing surface's route did not match the title the app publishes
defect.detail: The registry recorded app://ios/pairing; the running app's navigation bar identifier is 'Pair Mac'. Found by the capture tie pass once the ios-glass lane began recording each capture's target as a readback rather than as a label — which is the whole point of recording a readback. Route corrected to app://ios/pair-mac. Same class as DEF-007, where the Mac's Evals board shipped as Checks and only the registry still said Evals.

defect.title: every pairing action drew at label width where the design draws it at content width
defect.detail: `i1-phone-pairing.html` styles every pairing action `.cta`, which is `width:100%`. The build declared that with `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity)` on the `Button` — outside the style — so the layout frame stretched to full width while `PhoneProminentButtonStyle`/`PhoneStandardButtonStyle` still drew their background around a hugging label. Eleven call sites across the pairing flow, the connection banner and the triage commit bar. This is the same mistake `PhoneButtonStyle.swift`'s own doc comment already records for height, arriving through width: a geometry declaration outside the style grows the container and not the drawn control. No assertion could see it — the button's frame was already full width — so it was found by looking at the on-glass camera pre-prompt and typed-entry captures, where three centred pills sit in a full-width column. Fixed by moving the declaration inside both styles as `fillsWidth`. Guarded by `PhoneSurfaceTests.testAFullWidthPhoneButtonPaintsAFullWidthBand`, whose oracle is the painted band rather than any frame; armed 20 Aug 2026, where the pre-fix style painted 148pt inside a 393pt container.

defect.title: the paired-Mac settings action sits inside its notice card where the design draws it below
defect.detail: `i1-phone-pairing.html` §L draws the recovery action as a `<button class="cta">` sibling *after* the `wants` card, on all five Settings states that carry one. `PairedMacSettingsView` renders it as the last child inside `PhoneMessageBlock`'s own `VStack`, so the control shares the card's fill and inset. Width is corrected under DEF-024; placement is not, because moving it out changes the block's contract for all nine states in DESIGN.md §5 and is a design decision rather than a defect fix. Recorded against SURF-018.

defect.title: the never-paired settings surface stated the narrowing twice
defect.detail: `PairingCopy.settingsNeverPaired` carries `carriesNarrowing: true`, so `PhoneMessageBlock` rendered "This app queues items for review on your Mac. It cannot install, update or remove anything…" inside its block — and `PairedMacSettingsView` then rendered an About section that states the same sentence unconditionally. Both appear on the one surface a first-time user meets first, which reads as the app repeating itself rather than as emphasis. i1-phone-pairing.html states it once: §B puts it under the button with no About header, §I puts it under About. Fixed by suppressing the About section for a state whose own block carries it, read off the copy rather than off a case list. `PhoneSurfaceTests.testNarrowingIsRenderedWherePermissionIsDecided` now counts rather than existence-checks; armed 20 Aug 2026 against the pre-fix form, which read 2.

defect.title: the camera pre-prompt was toned neutral where the design tones it attention
defect.detail: i1-phone-pairing.html draws the pre-prompt in `.wants`, whose fill, border and headline are `--attnWash`/`--attnLine`/`--attn`, and §C annotates the reason: a caution before an irreversible grant is neither a failure nor decoration. `CameraPermissionView` passed `tone: .neutral` for `.notDetermined`, so the card rendered in the neutral grey the build uses for informational blocks. `PhoneMessageBlock.Tone.caution` already carried that exact rationale in its own doc comment and this surface was the one place it was earned and unused. Found by comparing the on-glass camera pre-prompt capture against a unit-scoped mock reference; the whole-page reference it replaced did not show this unit at all.

defect.title: the never-paired settings empty state drops the design's illustration and centring
defect.detail: i1-phone-pairing.html §B draws the never-paired state as `.pempty` — centred, with a 34px Mac glyph above the headline. `PairedMacSettingsView` renders it through `PhoneMessageBlock`, which is left-aligned and draws no glyph. The copy and the action are both correct and the narrowing is now stated once (DEF-026); what is missing is the illustration and the centring that make it read as an empty state rather than as a notice. Recorded against SURF-018 rather than fixed, because the same block draws eight other Settings states that the design does not centre.

defect.title: the iOS unit lane read an empty accessibility tree because the engine was off
defect.text: CAUSE FOUND AND FIXED 20 Aug 2026; this record replaces one that said the cause was unknown and named machine saturation as a candidate. The candidate was wrong. The process-wide accessibility engine was OFF, so SwiftUI's `_UIHostingView` built its accessibility container and vended an EMPTY element array — `accessibilityElements == []`, not nil — and every label assertion in the target read empty and reported its own honest verdict, `nothing was measured, so this proved nothing`. That is indistinguishable, from inside the suite, from a product that renders no copy. A probe settled it: calling `_AXSSetAutomationEnabled(true)` took the same hosted view's published element count from 0 to 1. THE ENGINE HAD BEEN ON BY ACCIDENT — something else on this machine had switched it on — which is why this suite was green for months while depending on ambient host state no file in this repo controls, and why it went red with no change to the branch. THREE CHANGES ARE THE FIX, and the third was found only because the first two were not enough. (1) `PhoneSurfaceTests` resolves `_AXSSetAutomationEnabled` out of `/usr/lib/libAccessibility.dylib` (falling back to `AccessibilityUtilities.framework`) via dlopen/dlsym and calls it once per process, before the first `host()`. (2) The walker reads `accessibilityElements` first, because SwiftUI publishes through the array and leaves `accessibilityElementCount()` at 0 — measured on iOS 26.5, where one hosted `Text` reported `accessibilityElements.count == 1` and `accessibilityElementCount() == 0` in the same breath, so reading only the indexed API walked past every element SwiftUI had. Those two took `make test-ios` from 52 failures to 0 — and then `make all`, run immediately afterwards on the same device, came back with 39. (3) THE STATE IS DEVICE-SCOPED AND THE CALL LANDS ON THE NEXT PROCESS, NOT THIS ONE. On a device left in the disabled state, the run that re-enables it fails a DETERMINISTIC set of 15 test cases — identical set, measured three times, verified with `comm` in both directions — and the run after it, with no change to anything, is clean. The 15 are exactly the cases that host a `ScrollView`; the tests that pass alongside them are geometry, counts and negative assertions, all of which an empty tree satisfies, so the green half of that run was vacuous too. `test-ios` therefore runs a throwaway single-test process before the graded one and discards its exit code. MEASURED END TO END: three consecutive runs with the call mutated to `(false)` drive `MCPRouter-Unit` into the disabled state (54 failures each, the whole suite red, which is correct for a dead engine); the very next `make test-ios`, with the warm-up in the recipe, is 36 tests and 0 failures in 1.4s. THE INSTRUMENT CHECK IS ITSELF INSTRUMENTED. `testTheAccessibilityEngineCanBeSwitchedOn` blocks on a probe that hosts `ScrollView { Text }` and reads it back through the same walk every other assertion uses, with a 20s deadline. Two narrower probes were built first and both were wrong in opposite directions, which is why the shape is stated rather than assumed: a bare `Text` read either way reports the engine live at t=0 of a run in which 15 cases went on to read empty, and a `ScrollView` read through the accessibility-container path alone reports the engine dead on a device where all 35 other tests pass. A probe that answers differently from the thing it stands for answers a different question. On a dead engine the deadline fires and the case fails with `no hosted Text published a label within 20s`, measured. ARMED THREE WAYS. (a) Renaming the symbol to `_AXSSetAutomationEnabledXXX` on a device whose engine is already live fails exactly one test — the instrument check — and leaves the other 35 green, which is correct for that arm and proves only the resolution assertion. (b) With the call mutated to `(false)`, the first run on `MCPRouter-Arm`, a device created for the arm, recorded 53 failures across 36 tests: that is what proves the other 35 depend on the engine. (c) The first run ever taken on `MCPRouter-Arm2`, a device whose engine had never been live, is 36 tests and 0 failures, so a fresh device needs no warm-up and only an explicitly disabled one does. Both arm devices were deleted afterwards; `make test-ios IOS_UNIT_DEVICE=<name>` recreates either. TWO HARDENING CHANGES from the investigation are kept and neither is the fix: `test-ios` creates and owns `MCPRouter-Unit` instead of sorting booted devices first — the exact picker DEF-020 condemned, still live in this recipe — and the walk retains every element it visits so `ObjectIdentifier` is unique among live objects as its use assumes. A third, waiting on a product surface's tree over a two-second deadline, was written, measured to change nothing, and removed: it cost 130 seconds a run and bought no measurement. The wait that IS kept differs from it in the one way that matters — it waits on a probe whose answer is known, so a timeout is a fact about the instrument rather than about the view. THE DEPENDENCY IS ON A PRIVATE SYMBOL, in the test target only, never linked into the app; the instrument check fails loudly if a future runtime renames it, so this target goes red rather than quietly empty. Carried as CASE-0126.

defect.title: four async package tests asserted on a deadline the machine could miss
defect.text:
Measured 20 Aug 2026. `make test` failed with 4 issues at a one-minute load average of ~700 and passed all 1473 tests in 179 suites at load 46, on the same source, minutes apart. The four were `ActivityReconnectTests` (`a reconnect over a feed that stays live releases its guard`), `DiscoverBoardTests` (`client.searchQueries.count` reading 1 where the baseline said 2), and `SettingsAndMenuBarTests` twice (`model.trackerState` still nil). An earlier run at the same load failed only the first, so the set was not stable either — which is what separated this from a product defect. A suite that reports a defect the product does not have is the failure this campaign has already paid for once, in DEF-029, where a dead instrument read as a dead product for ten consecutive runs.

CLOSED by making each wait a condition rather than a deadline, at three sites:

1. `ShellTestSupport.waitUntil` — ceiling 5s → 30s. It returns the moment the condition holds, so a passing test pays nothing for the larger bound; the bound exists only so a condition that never arrives fails instead of hanging. Five seconds was inside the scheduling noise of a contended host, which is the whole finding.
2. `ActivityReconnectTests.completes` — 2s → 30s, same argument. The defect it bounds is a call that *never* returns, so it exhausts any budget and a generous one costs only the time a genuine hang takes to report.
3. `DiscoverBoardTests.searchIsDebounced` — a fixed sleep replaced by two waits, because the claim has two halves and one sleep proved neither on a slow host. First a bounded wait for the debounce to fire at all; then a full debounce window of quiet with the count still at one, which is what rules out one request per keystroke. The second is a real quiet period rather than a deadline, so load cannot shorten it into a false pass — the wait on its own is satisfied by the *first* request and would pass against exactly the defect this test exists to catch.

Armed 20 Aug 2026, all three, each watched to fail with its own message: `waitUntil` at `.seconds(0)` reads `no poll ran at all`, `the poll died with the scene that started it` and `five keystrokes issued 0 requests`; `completes` at `.milliseconds(1)` reads `reconnect did not return while the feed stayed live`; and a `queryChanged()` inserted inside the quiet period reads `a later request arrived: five keystrokes issued 2 requests in total`.

The original trigger is not reproducible on demand from here — the load came from another project's Rust test binary, two node processes and `lsdiagnose` — so the fix is proven by the arms rather than by reproducing the contention.

defect.title: the Checks board is cross-subject where the design's is per-subject, so two of its actions have nowhere to go
defect.text: Found 20 Aug 2026 by the vocabulary differential, which reported `Edit cases…` and `Run again` in-design-not-build on this board, and recorded here rather than fixed because bolting those two buttons on would be the wrong repair. The design's pane at `prototype.html:885-891` is **one subject's** eval suite: it heads `pr-summariser · 8 cases`, subtitles `Ran 2 minutes ago against 0.4.1 in a scratch checkout`, and lists eight named cases with a verdict each. The built board is **cross-subject**: every server and skill, one row apiece, a reachability verdict per row, a filter, and `CheckCopy.runAllLabel` = `Re-check all…`. Those are two different surfaces wearing one route id, and the actions follow the framing — `Run again` re-runs the one suite on screen, which is what `Re-check all…` already does across all of them, so drawing both would be two names for one act (the failure DEF-012 records). `Edit cases…` opens an editor for a collection the app does not model: there is no eval case anywhere in `EvalsBoardModel`, so the button would offer a reading of something that does not exist — the same reason `Read first…` is a stated gap in DEF-011 rather than a drawn control. The divergence itself is the finding, and it is a scope question rather than a defect fix: the design specifies a per-subject eval board with named cases and an editor, and the app ships a cross-subject reachability board. Which one this product wants is the owner's call, and it is written up as a brief rather than decided here. Not guarded by an assertion, deliberately: there is nothing to assert until that call is made, and a test pinning today's cross-subject board would make the divergence harder to close rather than easier.

defect.title: the whole-repo gate discovered a missing environment forty minutes in, twice
defect.text:
Measured 20 Aug 2026 on two different worktrees the same afternoon. A fresh `git worktree` has no `node_modules` and no `dist`; `parity-selftest` is the last target `make all` runs, and its own environment check therefore fires only after lint, both builds, 1483 package tests, the iOS lane and the on-glass lane have all passed. Both runs came back `exit=2` on a tree where nothing was wrong with the code — roughly forty minutes each, twice.

It is a lane defect rather than a product one, and the shape is familiar: the gate was honest (it said `the MCP SDK is not installed. Run npm install.` rather than skipping) and it was honest at the wrong moment. A check that can only fail on the environment belongs where the environment is checked.

CLOSED by moving both checks into the `tools` target, which `all` runs first: `node_modules` must exist, and `dist/index.js` must exist because without it `parity-lane-selftest` SKIPS, and a skip is not a pass. Each names the command that fixes it.

Armed 20 Aug 2026 in a bare directory holding nothing but the Makefile: with no `node_modules` it exits 1 naming `npm install && npm run build`, and with `node_modules` present but no `dist` it exits 1 naming `npm run build` and saying why a skip is not a pass. defect.title: the OAuth parity lane failed once inside a full gate and has not reproduced
defect.detail:
parity-gate.sh, 20 Aug 2026 on main at e5755d0. The suite lane's citation run of scripts/acceptance/parity-oauth.sh exited non-zero and recorded `control-auth-post-http fail — the Swift router never reached the token endpoint`. The dedicated oauth lane, later in the same gate, ran the same script and recorded ok over 21 checks. The gate reported the row DIVERGED and printed 81 of 83.

WHY IT IS UNEXPLAINED, established 21 Aug 2026 from disk without re-running anything. The run survives as evidence/runs/parity-gate-2026-08-20-oauth-flake.log, written 20:39:30. Its line 163 is the whole of what the citation run reported: `FAIL scripts/acceptance/parity-oauth.sh    the gate reported findings`, and the next line is the following `ok` row. The script itself does not fail that quietly -- its failure branch (parity-oauth.sh:308-329) prints the POST /auth status, the browser hop, the tail of the router log and the first 20 requests the provider saw. Every one of those bytes existed and was discarded by the caller: `parity-suite.sh`'s `run_script` sent both streams to /dev/null at the time. So this defect is not a run that left no diagnostic, it is a run whose diagnostic the harness threw away, and no amount of re-reading the log can recover it. The instrument was repaired in commit 21d559b at 20:41:28 -- one minute and 58 seconds after this log was written, in the same commit that recorded the defect -- so `run_script` now keeps the log and prints its last 20 lines inline. A recurrence would therefore arrive with the cause attached. That is what closes this: the next occurrence, not more thought about this one. It stays open because there is still no cause and no reproduction; what changed is that the reason it could not be diagnosed is now known and no longer true.

One candidate mechanism examined and NOT adopted. The R9 lane reported (21 Aug 2026, via uds:/tmp/cc-socks/9881.sock) that a stale $TMPDIR/mcp-router-parity.lock had made a gate fail its manifest-check for a non-real reason. That is a different symptom -- a manifest-check failure before the comparison, against this defect's completed run that reached `control-auth-post-http` and recorded a row -- and parity-oauth.sh takes that same lock at line 126 and preflights every port at 143-145, so the two lanes inside one gate could not have overlapped. Recorded as ruled out rather than left unmentioned, so the next reader does not spend the lead twice.
defect.text:
Observed once, in one of two whole-gate runs, and not reproduced by: a standalone run of `parity-oauth.sh`, a second standalone run of it immediately afterwards (which exercised the same port-reuse wait, 9s and 12s), a standalone run of `parity-suite.sh`, or a second whole `parity-gate.sh` on the same tree. The second gate reported 82 of 83, 0 DIVERGED, and its suite lane reported the citation clean.

**What it is not.** The lane distinguishes an environment failure from a finding on purpose, and this was the finding branch: `record control-auth-post-http fail` at `parity-oauth.sh:329`, reached only when the reference side completed an authorization and the Swift side did not. An unbindable port exits 2 through `wait_for_ports_bindable` and records `blocked`, not `fail`, so the port-reuse race is ruled out by the code path that fired.

**Why it went undiagnosed, and what changed.** `parity-suite.sh`'s `run_script` sent both streams to `/dev/null` and printed `the gate reported findings` — a verdict with no evidence under it. The bytes naming which guard failed had already been thrown away by the time anyone read the gate's summary. `run_script` now keeps the log, prints its last 20 lines inline and names the file it kept, armed 20 Aug 2026 against a deliberately failing citation. A recurrence will say which of the 21 checks went red.

**Why the duplicate run stays.** `control-auth-post-http` is proven on the wire by its own lane and also cites the script, so the gate runs it twice. That is now documented in `parity-suite.sh` rather than deduplicated, because the duplicate is what caught this: a single run would have reported a clean 82 of 83 and nobody would have known. Both record under the same row id and a `fail` wins.

**Burn-in, 20 Aug 2026: 8 standalone runs of the lane, all green, 21 checks each.** Three immediately after the failure and five consecutively afterwards, plus one clean whole gate. One failure in roughly ten whole-lane executions, cause unrecoverable because that invocation's stdout was discarded. A green burn-in does not close this: the original failure is uninspectable, so the runs measure only that the lane is not reliably broken. What would close it is a captured reproduction, or a stated gate met — several consecutive whole gates including the cold port-reuse path — decided as its own question rather than inferred from a streak, which is the `install-launchd-watch` mistake this repository already paid for once (G1: name a fix per term and fix a bound IN ADVANCE, never a green streak). Not a UI defect and not a blocker on the cutover count — CASE-0036's measurement is the second run — but it is an unexplained non-determinism in the router or the lane, and it is recorded rather than absorbed.

defect.title: the blind-test pass flags three tests that do read after mutating, because the mutator's name is the observable's name
defect.detail:
`vacuity-check.py`'s blind pass reports `examined=1820 mutating=3 re-read-after=0 blind=3` over this test tree. All three read after the mutation: `restartIsIssuedBeforeTheStagingWrite` reads `WatchWorld.serverNames`, the log, `kicks.issued` and `WatchState.load`; `restartIsOwedBeforeTheWriteLands` reads `WatchState.load` inside the lock and `WatchWorld.serverNames` on both sides of the rename; `restartRechecksTheCamera` reads `model.entry.characters`. The heuristic looks for a read AFTER the last occurrence of a mutating verb, and in this product the verb `restart` is also the name of the thing being observed — `restartPending`, `restarted scratch-label` — so the last `restart` in the file sits inside the final assertion and nothing is textually after it. Recorded rather than acted on: the tests are correct as written, and rewording an assertion to satisfy a text heuristic would make the suite worse. The pass is still worth running; 3 of 1820 is a reviewable rate, and it is the check that would have caught 26 of 32 on the campaign it was built from.

CAUSE CORRECTED 21 Aug 2026; the diagnosis recorded above was wrong. It said the mutator's name is the observable's name (`restart` inside `restartPending`). Measured against 0.9.2's actual patterns, that cannot happen: the mutator scan at vacuity-check.py:180 requires `(?<![A-Za-z0-9_])` + verb + `\w*\s*\(`, so `state.restartPending == false` never matches for want of the call parenthesis. The real cause is that the seven default readers are all snake_case -- list_, get_, read_, fetch_, sample_, count_, load_ -- and the nine default mutators mostly are too (stop_all, stop_runner, clear_, cancel_). This is a camelCase Swift codebase, so NEITHER side could fire. The pass examined 1657 test bodies and found 3 mutating, 0 re-reading and 3 blind: `blind=3` reads as almost nothing wrong, and meant almost nothing looked at. The denominator was printed and nobody read 3-of-1657 as the alarm it was. Fixed by declaring the project's own vocabulary, which 0.9.2 added for exactly this: campaign.json now carries `blindVocabulary` with 14 camelCase mutators and 13 readers, and the pass reports examined=1657 mutating=320 re-read-after=232 blind=88, with the vocabulary it used printed above the findings. Two of the three original findings resolved on their real reads (`WatchState.load(`, `WatchWorld.read(`). The third, restartRechecksTheCamera, stays flagged and correctly so for a verb heuristic: its only reads are property comparisons -- `model.step`, `model.entry.characters` -- which carry no verb at all. That is the ceiling of this instrument rather than a defect in the test, and it is why the 88 is a worklist and not a verdict: the vocabulary is hand-declared and unvalidated. Of the 21 findings the tool prints, 15 carry a @Test attribute and 5 are fixture helpers in dedicated client files that 0.9.2's per-file helper heuristic does not exclude, because it keys on a function being called more than once in its OWN file and these are called from their importers.

defect.title: the campaign's own defect ids named two different defects each, because the staging file numbered from its own length
defect.detail:
`campaign.py` keeps defects in `inventory.json` under a `defect` list, and `add` assigns the next id from that list. `defects.in.json` is an input file. Twelve defects found in the sittings of 19 and 20 Aug were written straight into the input file with hand-written ids taken from that file's own length, which had stopped tracking the registry at DEF-006. The result: DEF-007 through DEF-018 each named one defect in the registry and a different one in the staging file, and neither file said so.

Visible symptom, and the only reason it was caught: `RUN-2026-08-20.md` contains 'DEF-011 is the finding worth acting on ... Cleanup's' at line 96 and 'DEF-011 - the rendered-quality gate has never been able to run' at line 481, in one document, meaning two unrelated things. This is `capture-lineage`'s failure mode moved from pictures to identifiers: a name binding to two subjects with nothing checking the binding.

Fixed by renumbering the twelve staged defects to DEF-034..DEF-045, merging them into the registry, and rewriting the fifteen references that meant the staged numbering. Every renumbered record carries `stagedAs` naming its old local id, so a reader meeting the old number in an untouched artifact can resolve it. The remaining 74 references were checked one at a time and meant the registry defect they already named.

A fourth lesson, from the third instance's cleanup rather than from the collision itself. Reconstructing the concurrent session's two entries welded `text: ""` and `note: ""` onto both, and the first renumbering pass then used `"text" in d` to tell the two writers' entries apart -- so the artifact defeated the discriminator that would have caught it. Both authors independently read the empty values as harmless because they carried no content. The hazard is shape, not content: a membership test reads a key's PRESENCE, and an empty string defeats `"text" in d` exactly as thoroughly as a populated one would. `campaign.py add` injects only `id`, `status`, `evidence` and `armed`, so that key-shape occurred on exactly the two reconstructed entries and was traceable; the keys were stripped and the pass re-run discriminating on `title`. Recorded because "empty therefore harmless" is a reasonable-sounding wrong answer that both sessions gave.
defect.found-by: id-collision check while filing the design-size fidelity findings
defect.note:
SECOND INSTANCE, 20 Aug 2026, in the case registry rather than the defect registry, and it landed the same way. A helper reported `next case id: CASE-0145` while cases.json already held CASE-0149 and CASE-0150; campaign.py's own `next_id` is max+1 and would have said CASE-0151, so the number that was trusted did not come from it. `add` takes an explicit id through `setdefault` and therefore appends a second entry rather than refusing, so CASE-0149 and CASE-0150 each came to name two cases -- an iOS Settings structural case against REQ-005 and a RouterCore write-failure case against REQ-019 -- and the `set` calls that followed wrote onto the pre-existing pair.
Caught by an evidence-existence audit rather than by any gate: the new cases printed `3 evidence` where two were supplied. Restored from `git show HEAD:` (both pre-existing entries are byte-identical to HEAD again, verified by dict comparison) and the new pair renumbered to CASE-0153 and CASE-0154. The registry is sparse -- 74 gaps between 1 and 152 -- so a free-looking number is not evidence that it is free, and only max+1 is.

THIRD INSTANCE, the same evening, and this one had two writers rather than one. A second Claude session working the same campaign allocated DEF-047 and DEF-048 at about 23:30 (the SDK -32603 message discard, and a detector defect in vacuity-check.py's blind pass) and committed planning/test-campaign as a directory in 6bdeea4, which also swept up this session's in-progress registry edits. This session allocated DEF-047 and DEF-048 for different defects minutes later, from a read taken before that commit landed. Resolved by renumbering THIS session's pair to DEF-049 and DEF-050 -- the later allocation moves, and the session that moves is the one that can enumerate its own references, which is the only reason the choice is safe rather than arbitrary. The peer's entries were not edited.
Note for anyone reading the mechanism: `add` assigns from the registry list, so two writers holding a stale read get the same number, and no gate in the campaign detects it. The detection here was a peer message, and before that an evidence-existence audit; neither is a gate. campaign.py could refuse an explicit id that already exists -- `add` currently takes one through `setdefault` and appends a duplicate instead.

defect.title: the Swift MCP SDK discards an upstream's error message for code -32603, so the router reports less than the reference does
defect.detail: Found 20 Aug 2026 while building R8's gate against both routers. Against a fixture returning `-32603` with the message `Internal error: Authentication required`, the reference records `MCP error -32603: Internal error: Authentication required` and the Swift router records `[-32603] Internal error`. The upstream's own message is gone. CAUSE, cited exactly: modelcontextprotocol/swift-sdk 0.12.1, `Sources/MCP/Base/Error.swift:217-240`. The decoder reads the server's `message`, then maps the code — `-32700`, `-32600`, `-32601` and `-32602` each pass `unwrapDetail(message)`, and `-32603` alone passes `unwrapDetail(nil)`. `unwrapDetail(fallback)` returns `data.detail` when present and the fallback otherwise, so a server that answers -32603 with a message and no `data.detail` has its message discarded, and `Error.swift:91` renders `"Internal error" + (detail.map { ": \($0)" } ?? "")` as the bare canonical name. -32603 is the code servers use for an arbitrary application error, so it is the one that loses the most. TWO consequences: for the whole class of -32603 upstream errors the Swift router tells the user strictly less than the reference does; and R8's Swift half cannot detect a credential refusal at all, because there is no text left to match. This is a coverage gap in the parity suite as much as a defect in the SDK — no parity scenario had ever exercised a JSON-RPC error carrying a detailed message, which is why 82 proven rows never saw it. Remedies, none taken: report upstream and take a fixed release; pin a patched fork; or read the JSON-RPC error before the SDK types it, which needs a seam below the client.

defect.title: test-campaign 0.9.1's blind-mutation pass is dominated by its own verb configuration on this codebase, in both directions
defect.detail:
DETECTOR DEFECT, recorded so its numbers are not published as product findings. `vacuity-check.py`'s `blind` pass asks whether any READER appears after the last MUTATING call in a test body, both matched by name prefix. Run with the shipped defaults it reports `examined=1820 mutating=3 blind=3` — and all three are false: DEFAULT_READERS is snake_case (`load_`, `get_`, `read_`, `list_`) while this is a camelCase Swift codebase, so NO Swift reader can ever match, and the three `mutating` hits matched the token `restart` in their own function names. Both flagged WatchRestartTests cases read extensively after the mutation. Run with a hand-derived camelCase verb list it reports `examined=1834 mutating=258 re-read-after=158 blind=100`. Two of the flagged real tests were read in full and BOTH re-read: `undoRestoresTheItem` calls `queue.all()` three times after `model.remove(...)`, and `resetReindexesAnIndexFailure` reads `client.calls` after `board.reset(...)`. Neither `all` nor `calls` was in the list. Of the 20 findings the script prints, only 6 are `@Test` functions at all; the other 14 are test doubles and helpers, because the population is every `func` in any file with `test` in its path. CONCLUSION: on this codebase the pass measures the verb list rather than the suite, and no verb list derived by hand is evidence of anything. It is recorded, not published, and the campaign claims no blind-mutation number. The pass's other two arms — `unclassed` and `uncensused` — are exact and are kept.

ADDRESSED UPSTREAM in 0.9.2, confirmed by running it 21 Aug 2026. Commit 28ecd67 (`the blind-mutation check was measuring itself`) fixes four detector defects that each RAISED the blind count, and the pass now prints the vocabulary it used above its findings -- `vocabulary: defaults + campaign.blindVocabulary — 22 mutator(s), 20 reader(s)` followed by the reader list -- which was this defect's complaint: a number published without saying what configuration produced it. The denominator also moved, 1841 to 1657, because fixture helpers are no longer counted as tests. Left open rather than closed: the residual named on DEF-040 sits in the same pass.

SUPERSEDED 21 Aug 2026 by DEF-055. The specific claim here — snake_case DEFAULT_READERS against a camelCase Swift codebase, giving examined=1820 mutating=3 blind=3 with all three false — was resolved by declaring campaign.json's blindVocabulary, which 0.9.2 reads. The general claim, that no hand-derived verb list is evidence of anything, is not resolved; it is now MEASURED rather than asserted. DEF-055 carries that measurement (7 of 7 sampled findings false, four named mechanisms, a two-way arm) and is the entry to read. Recorded as superseded rather than closed: the finding was real and its successor is open.

defect.text: `MCPRouterCLI index` reports a clean index and exits 0 when the manifest write does not land, and prints two counts that disagree with each other in the same output.
defect.note:
Found by a denial control in the effect-witness pass rather than by reading code: `bin/witness-arm-denial.sh` points the CLI at a router home with mode dr-x------, which the process may read and traverse but not write. `index --force` then prints `ok    witness-fixture (1 tools)`, prints `0 tools cached -> /tmp/.../manifest.json` eight lines later, and exits 0 over a manifest.json that does not exist.

Cause: ManifestIndexer.record at RouterCore/Service/ServicePorts.swift:341 calls `try? ManifestIO.save(...)`. ManifestIO.save throws correctly and its own doc comment is careful about the disk-full case -- it deliberately leaves the temp file behind as evidence -- but all three call sites discard the error (AuthRoutes.swift:120, WatchIndexing.swift:150, ServicePorts.swift:341). The verb's closing count is honest, because MCPRouterCLI.swift:167-173 re-reads the manifest from disk to compute it; nothing compares that count against the per-server line above it.

The same `try?` on the control-API path is already characterised and deliberate -- ControlApproveDispatchTests.approveWithARefusingFileSystem pins the 200, registered in spec-P1 section 8, as R5's shipped behaviour that P1 does not move. This is the second call site, and until CASE-0153, CASE-0154 and CASE-0151 no test in the repo named ManifestIndexer at all, which is why the swallow survived here after being characterised there. The iOS side of the same requirement was found and fixed -- PhoneStorageFailureTests covers `try? await store.save(mac)` letting a success surface render over a refused write.

Left open-owner rather than fixed in campaign: propagating the error changes the CLI's exit code, which is a shipped-contract decision, and the project has already taken the opposite decision once on a sibling path. CASE-0153, CASE-0154 and CASE-0151 characterise today's behaviour so the day someone changes it, the change is deliberate.

defect.text: A ShellTests assertion on the `.success` reindex scenario compared a non-optional Int to nil, so it was always true and read nothing.
defect.note:
`#expect(result.tools != nil, ...)` at ShellTests.swift:133. `ReindexResult.tools` is a non-optional `Int` (MCPRouterKit/Control/Models.swift:263), so the comparison could not fail. The Swift compiler emitted `comparing non-optional value of type 'Int' to 'nil' always returns true` on every build of the test target; it was the only such warning in the suite.

The intent was stated in the comment directly above it -- `.success` is distinguished from `.populated` by `a reindex that comes back with no error and a tool count` -- so the assertion was one character from doing its job. Repaired to `result.tools == 14`, the value FixtureControlAPIClient+Writes.swift:33 overrides for `.success`, which discriminates against the base `reindex-failure.json` fixture it starts from (`{"tools":0,"error":"fetch failed"}`).

Armed in evidence/arming/CASE-0152.arming.log: with the override changed to 0 the assertion goes red (`(result.tools -> 0) == 14`), and the log records that the pre-repair form would have stayed green under the same mutation.

defect.text: witness-worklist.py counts a pair as judgeable on the reference alone, so a surface with no build capture inflates the comparable fraction.
defect.note:
DETECTOR DEFECT, recorded so its number is not published as a product finding. `witness-worklist.py:90` is `judgeable = [p for p in pairs if p.get("reference")]` -- it tests the reference half and never the shot half. SURF-009 (Mac menu-bar popover) has `shot: null` and an explicit `reason: build half uncaptured` in pairs.json, and is still counted, so the script reported `pairs=20 judgeable=17 comparable fraction: 85%` where the honest figure is 16 of 20, 80%.
The script already defends the mirror-image failure and its own comment says why: a campaign reported 20 judgeable pairs whose references were all unrendered .html paths, and it now demotes those to unjudgeable with a named reason. The shot side has no equivalent test.
Consequence here is one point of over-report and no false verdict, because capture-lineage.py computes judgeable from captures that exist and reported JUDGED 16 of 16 -- the two gates disagree by exactly this surface, and the disagreement is what found it. A campaign relying on the worklist alone would carry an uncompared surface inside a comparable fraction.
Filed against the skill's script rather than this repo, so it is not fixed here.
defect.detail:
STILL PRESENT in 0.9.2, re-measured 21 Aug 2026 and the gap widened by one. witness-worklist.py reports `pairs=20 judgeable=17 WITHOUT a reference=3` and a comparable fraction of 85%, while capture-lineage.py --gate on the same registry reports `published captures: 16` and `JUDGED 16 of 16 judgeable (100%)`. Two gates in one skill version disagree about the judgeable denominator, 17 against 16, and neither names the other's population.

CAUSE PINNED 21 Aug 2026. The disagreeing member is SURF-009, the Mac menu-bar popover, and it is the only one: witness-worklist's judgeable set and capture-lineage's judged set are identical apart from it. SURF-009 has a rendered design of record on disk (evidence/shots/mock/SURF-009.png), which is the sole condition witness-worklist tests, so it counts as the 17th judgeable pair. It has NO build capture at all — the popover cannot be opened without activating MCPRouter, which this campaign never does — so it never enters capture-lineage's population, which is built from published captures. capture-lineage therefore reports 'JUDGED 16 of 16 judgeable (100%)' on a registry holding 17 judgeable surfaces.

That is the defect's whole shape, and it is the campaign's own first failure mode occurring INSIDE a gate written to prevent it: a denominator built from what was captured rather than from what was enumerated reads 100% precisely when a surface was never photographed. The direction is the dangerous one — an uncaptured surface raises the percentage instead of lowering it.

Nothing is concealed in this campaign's own record: SURF-009 carries a shotNote naming the constraint, its three cases (CASE-0004, CASE-0006, CASE-0109) are n/a with the reason, and evidence/shots/pairs.json carries shot:null. The defect is that a reader of the gate line alone would not know to look for any of it. Remains open-detector: the fix is in the skill's scripts, which are not edited from this repo.

defect.title: evidence-page.py and campaign.py's ledger writer both skip the defect registry, so no published artifact lists a defect
defect.detail:
DETECTOR DEFECT in test-campaign 0.9.1, found 20 Aug 2026 by the concurrent session at uds:/tmp/cc-socks/9881.sock and confirmed here against the artifact rather than against a model of it. The string `defect` does not appear as a registry key anywhere in evidence-page.py; measured with grep, zero occurrences. Its `

Defects

` at line 521 renders `[c for c in cases if state_of(c.get('status')) == 'fail']` -- failing CASES -- and the nav counter at line 305 is `counts['fail']`, the same population. So the page's Defects section counts 3 (the failing cases CASE-0010, CASE-0040, CASE-0110) while inventory.json holds 11 open defects, and the two numbers are about different things. MEASURED against the regenerated 124100-byte evidence.html: of the 11 open defects, 8 appear ZERO times -- DEF-008, DEF-040, DEF-041, DEF-042, DEF-043, DEF-047, DEF-048, DEF-051. The 3 that do appear are there by accident of prose: DEF-001 in two failing case notes and one passing one, DEF-033 and DEF-049 each inside a single PASSING case's note, rendered by the per-case table rather than by the Defects section. The peer reported 11 invisible; the true figure is 8, because writing a defect id into a case note is a convention doing a gate's job and it happened to fire three times. `campaign.py check` also exits 0 with all 11 open, so no gate holds on the registry either. This is the skill's own first-named failure mode -- covering a subset and reporting it as the whole -- arriving in its publisher: the gated half of the campaign is sound and the ungated half is the half people look at. The fix belongs in the installed skill (render inv['defect'], and count open defects in the nav), not in this repo; recorded rather than patched, precedent DEF-048 and DEF-051. SECOND PUBLISHER, same root cause, measured here: `campaign.py`'s own ledger writer (campaign.py:1210-1240) loads `inventory` and never reads `inventory['defect']` either, so ledger.md names zero defects across its 83 lines. Its header line is sharper than an omission -- it prints `73 pass . 3 fail . 0 skip . 4 n/a . 0 open . armed 73/73`, where `0 open` is the count of open CASES, on a campaign holding 12 open defects. A reader who takes that line at face value reads a campaign with nothing outstanding. ledger.md is generated rather than hand-kept, so it cannot be corrected in this repo: a fix that patched only evidence-page.py would leave the ledger short, and both publishers need to read the registry.

defect.title: strict-check.py omits effect-witness from EFFECT_RUNGS, so the ladder's top rung scores as 'only proves something rendered' and the gate penalises the hardest available work
defect.detail: DETECTOR DEFECT in test-campaign 0.9.1, found 21 Aug 2026 while accounting for the 19 unchecked cases. Two scripts in the SAME skill version disagree about what asserts an effect, and both carry a comment claiming to define it. `campaign.py:123` -- `EFFECT_RUNGS = ('outcome', 'metamorphic', 'effect-witness', 'raster-visual', 'interactive-glass')`, under the comment `A critical flow promises an effect. Only these rungs assert one.` `strict-check.py:54` -- `EFFECT_RUNGS = {'outcome', 'metamorphic', 'raster-visual', 'interactive-glass'}`, under `Only these assert an effect`, and its comment ends `See campaign.py` -- pointing at the file it contradicts. MEASURED here: this campaign holds 4 effect-witness cases (CASE-0145 through CASE-0148), all pass, all armed, each carrying an independent kernel recorder (the shell's $! plus the child's own getppid(); lsof(8)'s LISTEN row and the accepted ESTABLISHED half; stat(2) inode and mtime) and each backed by a denial control that flips it. strict-check.py scores all four into the `only proves something rendered` bucket, which is why that bucket reads 12 when only 8 cases sit at a structural rung. The gate therefore reports CHECKED 61 of 80; counting effect-witness as campaign.py does, and as SKILL.md's ladder does, the figure is 65 of 80 (81%). The consequence is worse than an understatement. effect-witness is the most expensive rung in the ladder -- it requires a recorder the product does not control, a non-zero count, and a sabotage control -- and a campaign optimising for the strict number is steered AWAY from it toward `outcome`, which costs less and scores more. A gate that pays less for harder evidence inverts the incentive the whole skill exists to create. The fix is one token in strict-check.py:54. It belongs in the installed skill and is recorded rather than patched from here, precedent DEF-048, DEF-051 and DEF-052. The ratchet is deliberately left at the gate's own 61 rather than raised to the corrected 65: the ratchet is the gate's record of itself, and editing it to a number the gate does not compute would be the campaign marking its own homework. RESOLVED 21 Aug 2026, and the fix predates the finding. test-campaign 0.9.2 is installed at ~/.claude/plugins/cache/fledgeling-plugins/test-campaign/0.9.2 and its strict-check.py:59 already reads `EFFECT_RUNGS = {'outcome', 'metamorphic', 'effect-witness', 'raster-visual', 'interactive-glass'}`, under a comment naming the same incentive inversion independently derived here: `a campaign that built a real witness watched its strict score stay flat, which is precisely the wrong incentive to attach to the most expensive rung.` Confirmed by running it: 0.9.2 reports CHECKED 65 of 80 (81%) with 8 in the rendered-only bucket, against 0.9.1's 61 of 80 and 12 -- exactly the four effect-witness cases and no others. This session had been running 0.9.1's scripts throughout while 0.9.2 sat installed alongside it, which is the reason the defect was visible here at all.

defect.title: attach-shots --apply would attach the design mock render as the build's surface shot for 11 surfaces, and its report names the surface rather than the file
defect.detail: DETECTOR DEFECT in test-campaign 0.9.2, found 21 Aug 2026. attach-shots.py iterates every image under evidence/shots and assigns `hit['shot'] = rel` on each match, last write wins, with no preference for a build capture over a design render. This campaign keeps six directories under evidence/shots (16 root, 8 design-size, 16 fidelity, 9 ios, 17 mock, 11 mock-hidpi), so for SURF-001 the candidates in iteration order are SURF-001.build.png, SURF-001.shell.png, mock/SURF-001.png, mock-hidpi/SURF-001.full.png -- and the last one wins. MEASURED for SURF-001, SURF-002 and SURF-006: `--apply` would repoint each surface's `shot` from its build capture to `evidence/shots/mock-hidpi/SURF-00N.full.png`, which is the render of the DESIGN, not the build. That is the skill's own headline failure mode -- publishing a picture of one thing under the name of another -- arriving in a sibling of the plane built to prevent it, and it would do so while every other gate stayed green, because capture-lineage.py gates the 16 captures cited by CASES and the surface wall is a different population. The report compounds it: the UNCORROBORATED block prints surface ids (SURF-001 ... SURF-011) rather than the file each verdict is about, so a reader sees eleven surfaces apparently lacking provenance when in fact each surface's ACTUAL `shot` field points at a corroborated build capture and the complaint is about a mock render nobody intended to attach. Distinguishing the two costs a re-derivation of the matcher by hand. Recorded rather than patched, precedent DEF-048, DEF-051, DEF-052 and DEF-053. The campaign's standing refusal to run `--apply` here predates this and was based on the DEF-006 mis-wire; it now has a measured mechanism behind it. Separately closed while investigating: this campaign's design-size captures carried their provenance in a second manifest, evidence/shots/design-size/captures.json, in a different schema ({captures:[...]} against the root's bare list) that no gate reads. Its 8 entries were merged into the root manifest with `target` derived from the root's declared target for the same subject and corroborated by each capture's own windowTitleReadback -- Servers, Activity, Skills, Discover, Inbox, Checks, Cleanup, Settings, every one matching -- recorded at capture time, and each carries `targetDerivedFrom` saying so. That was the campaign's own inconsistency and is fixed here; it was not the cause of the 11.

defect.title: vacuity-check's blind-mutation pass examines non-tests and mis-reads Swift idiom; 7 of 7 sampled findings are false positives
defect.detail:
Measured 2026-08-21 against test-campaign 0.9.2 on app/Tests. The pass reports examined=1661 mutating=320 blind=88. Two structural errors and two idiom errors inflate that number.

STRUCTURAL. (1) It scans every `func`, not every test. Restricted to swift-testing's own discriminator (a func whose nearest preceding annotation is @Test) the denominator is 1531, not 1661: 130 of the examined functions are not tests. (2) Its helper exclusion at vacuity-check.py:162 is file-scoped — a name is a helper only if called more than once in the file that declares it. A shared stub declared in TestSupport.swift and called from other files therefore reads as a test, so MemoryFileSystem's `write`, `removeItem` and `moveItem`, HTTPStub's `stop` and WatchTestSupport's `remove` are each counted as a blind test. 21 of the 88 are support-file functions.

IDIOM, on the mutator side. (3) The lookbehind `(?<![A-Za-z0-9_])` cannot exclude a dot, so a Swift enum case constructor matches a mutator verb: `ServerRowAction.forServer(s, pendingAuth: nil) == .reset(.clearPlacard)` reports ServerPresentationTests::trippedOutranksHeld as mutating via 'reset', where `.reset` is the expected VALUE inside the assertion. 41 of 72 re-measured findings are dot-prefixed. (4) It takes the last mutator by source POSITION and calls everything after it the tail, which misreads three Swift constructs: a mutator inside the assertion (`await #expect(throws: Never.self) { try await store.delete() }` — nothing can follow it by construction), a mutator in a `defer` block (source-early, execution-last, so the whole test body reads as 'after'), and a mutator as the last statement of a loop body whose observation is the next iteration (CallbackLifecycleTests::stopReleasesTheSocket rebinds the port ten times; the read of cycle N is the start() of cycle N+1).

SAMPLE. Of the 15 findings with zero assertions after the last mutator — the highest-yield stratum — 9 were read in full. Two (DiscoveryTests::servers, CapabilityPlateTests::install) are helpers. All 7 remaining are real tests that do observe after mutating, through idioms no reader verb names: `client.calls.last?.operation`, `seen.filter { ... }`, a rebind that throws. Precision on that stratum is 0 of 7.

ARMED, two ways, evidence/arming/blind-mutation.arming.log. A probe @Test that mutates and never observes was added and removed: blind moved 88 -> 89 -> 88 and examined/mutating moved by exactly 1 each time. The check does bite; it is the false-positive rate that is at issue, not the sensitivity.

NOT REMEDIED BY VOCABULARY. The reader side is deliberately loose because a false reader match suppresses a finding. Adding this codebase's read idioms (`calls`, `operation`, `filter`) would lower the number without improving what the pass knows, and the terms are generic enough to suppress true findings too. The 88 stands recorded as a worklist with its measured precision beside it rather than tuned to look better.

defect.title: campaign.py's ledger writer prints only cases filed under a surface, silently dropping 8 of 80 — including all four effect-witness cases
defect.detail:
Measured 2026-08-21, test-campaign 0.9.2. `ledger.md`'s header line reads `80 cases` and `73 pass · 3 fail · 0 skip · 4 n/a`; its table carries 72 rows. The eight absent cases are CASE-0145, 0146, 0147, 0148 (lane router-daemon) and CASE-0151, 0152, 0153, 0154 (lane swiftui). All eight pass.

MECHANISM, exact. The writer at campaign.py:1218-1241 buckets every case with `by_surface.setdefault(c.get('surface', '—'), [])`, so a case whose `surface` is absent lands under the literal key `'—'`. It then emits rows with `for s in inventory['surface']: for c in by_surface.get(s['id'], [])`. `'—'` is not a surface id, so that bucket is never visited and its contents are never printed. Nothing warns; the count in the header comes from a different code path than the rows beneath it, which is why the two disagree without either being flagged.

WHAT IS LOST. CASE-0145 through CASE-0148 are this campaign's four `effect-witness` cases — the rung that required building a recorder outside the product, and the most expensive evidence in the run. They are absent from the ledger entirely. A reader of ledger.md cannot learn that the campaign has an effect-witness rung at all.

DIRECTION. The eight dropped are all passes, so the table under-states the work rather than over-stating it. That makes it the safer direction, and it does not make it safe: a reader counting 72 rows against a stated 80 meets an unexplained gap of exactly the kind this campaign is written to make impossible, and the campaign's own rule is that every sweep prints its denominator.

SCOPE. Ledger-specific. evidence.html renders all eight (5 to 11 references each, measured by grep), so the HTML page is correct and only the markdown artifact is affected. Distinct from DEF-052, which is about the defect registry being absent from BOTH artifacts; this one is about cases, in one artifact, via a different mechanism.

NOT FIXED FROM HERE: campaign.py lives in the installed skill cache, not this repo.

defect.title: the vendored fledgeling-plugins submodule is test-campaign 0.5.0 while every gate in this campaign ran from the machine's 0.9.2 cache
defect.detail:
Measured 2026-08-21. `.gitmodules` vendors `.claude/plugins/fledgeling-plugins` at `main`, and `planning/features-to-triage/LEDGER.md`'s allocation notes state the reason: 'a runner reads mockup-fidelity, mac-craft, design-craft and ux-craft at a repo-relative path rather than depending on the machine.'
